name: Back extension
angleNote: The trunk's bend to the legs: 0° = body straight (top), 90° = folded down over the pads. Lifting makes it smaller. With the back straight all of the bend is at the hips; the back-rounding slider moves part of it into the lower back.

strength.note: Relative isometric hip-extension torque vs hip flexion, peak about 53°, measured standing with the knee slightly bent (tested −29° to 74°; deeper hip flexion is held flat at the 74° value, which is extrapolation). Relative curve = cos(C2·(θ − C3)) with the 18–25-year-old male means of Table 3, as for the glute kickback. Peak 202 Nm per hip (the same table's C1, young men, scaled to 73 kg and 1.75 m).
strength.source: Anderson DE, Madigan ML, Nussbaum MA (2007). Maximum voluntary joint torque as a function of joint angle and angular velocity: model development and application to the lower limb. J Biomech 40(14):3105–3113. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2007.03.022

strength.note: Isometric lumbar extension of 56 men by lumbar flexion: about 238, 296, 345, 375, 405, 432 and 465 Nm at 0°, 12°, 24°, 36°, 48°, 60° and 72° (read off Fig. 4; women about 135–240 Nm). Strongest fully flexed: the back extensors are longer there, and the ligaments and discs, stretched, add to the measured torque. The OpenSim lumbar spine model (Christophy et al. 2012) supports that: its back muscles' active capacity (force × moment arm, summed over iliocostalis, longissimus, multifidus and quadratus lumborum) is highest near upright and falls about 24% from 10° to 60° of flexion, while the measured strength rises by about 45%. So a rounded back makes the lower back look strong largely by handing load to passive tissues, which this model doesn't separate. Arched (below 0°), not measured by Graves et al.: the points at −10° and −20° follow the OpenSim lumbar spine model's active back-muscle capacity, which falls 6% and 14% from upright to 10° and 20° of extension.
strength.source: Graves JE, Pollock ML, Carpenter DM, Leggett SH, Jones A, MacMillan M, Fulton M (1990). Quantitative assessment of full range-of-motion isometric lumbar extension strength. Spine 15(4):289–294. doi:10.1097/00007632-199004000-00008 (Fig. 4: 56 men, MedX machine, seated, pelvis and femurs restrained, torso weight counterbalanced); Christophy M, Faruk Senan NA, Lotz JC, O'Reilly OM (2012). A musculoskeletal model for the lumbar spine. Biomech Model Mechanobiol 11:19–34. doi:10.1007/s10237-011-0290-6 (OpenSim model, MIT licence; data/opensim/lumbar-muscles.json)

muscles.name: Gluteus maximus
muscles.note: Main hip extensor. On the 45° Roman chair it was as active as in the Romanian deadlift over the whole lift and more active in the top part, where the 45° bench keeps the load on (Andersen et al., 15 trained women, 6-RM loads).
muscles.source: Andersen V, Pedersen H, Fimland MS, Shaw M, Solstad TEJ, Stien N, Cumming KT, Saeterbakken AH (2021). Comparison of muscle activity in three single-joint, hip extension exercises in resistance-trained women. J Sports Sci Med 20:181–187. doi:10.52082/jssm.2021.181 (relative differences only; weights here are estimates)

muscles.name: Hamstrings
muscles.note: With the knees straight they are long and strong hip extensors. Biceps femoris activity on the 45° Roman chair was 71% above the Romanian deadlift's (Andersen et al.).
muscles.source: Andersen V, Pedersen H, Fimland MS, Shaw M, Solstad TEJ, Stien N, Cumming KT, Saeterbakken AH (2021). Comparison of muscle activity in three single-joint, hip extension exercises in resistance-trained women. J Sports Sci Med 20:181–187. doi:10.52082/jssm.2021.181 (relative differences only; weights here are estimates)

muscles.name: Adductor magnus
muscles.note: Its rear part is a strong hip extensor when the hip is bent.
muscles.source: Bourne MN, Williams MD, Opar DA, Al Najjar A, Kerr GK, Shield AJ (2017). Impact of exercise selection on hamstring muscle activation. Br J Sports Med 51(13):1021–1028. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2015-095739 (24 men, 10 exercises)

muscles.name: Erector spinae
muscles.note: Hold the lower back against the upper body's weight; with a rounded back they move it. The same moment at every rounding for the same trunk position, but measured stronger when flexed (Graves et al.), partly because ligaments and discs then carry some of it. Their activity was the same in the Roman chair, the Romanian deadlift and a seated back-extension machine (Andersen et al.).
muscles.source: Andersen V, Pedersen H, Fimland MS, Shaw M, Solstad TEJ, Stien N, Cumming KT, Saeterbakken AH (2021). Comparison of muscle activity in three single-joint, hip extension exercises in resistance-trained women. J Sports Sci Med 20:181–187. doi:10.52082/jssm.2021.181 (relative differences only; weights here are estimates)

phases.name: Top
phases.text: Body straight. On the 45° bench the load stays on here; on the horizontal bench this is the hardest part. Going past straight arches the lower back.

phases.name: Mid-range
phases.text: On the 45° bench the trunk is horizontal at 45° of hip bend, where its weight has the longest lever.

phases.name: Bottom
phases.text: Folded over the pads. On the horizontal bench the trunk hangs nearly straight down: little torque. On the 45° bench it points 45° below horizontal at 90°.

variants.name: 45° Roman chair
variants.notes: Body weight, or a plate hugged to the chest. The upper body's weight has its longest lever when the trunk is horizontal (45° of hip bend here), and the lift still carries load at the top.

variants.name: 45° Roman chair, plate behind the head
variants.notes: The same plate held behind the head sits about 0.26 m further from the hips than at the chest: about 60% more torque from the plate.

variants.name: Horizontal back extension
variants.notes: Lying face down with the hips on the pad. The trunk is horizontal at the top, so the hardest point is the end of the lift, where the hips are also weaker (less bent).

placement.label: Back rounding (− = arched)
placement.hint: 0° = back straight (neutral): the whole bend is at the hips, the glutes and hamstrings do the lifting and the back muscles only hold. Rounding takes part of the bend into the lower back: for the same trunk position the hips bend less (the glutes and hamstrings work shorter, where they are weaker) and the back muscles work flexed, where they measure stronger, partly because ligaments and discs take up load. The upper body's moment about the lower back changes little (the rounded trunk sits a bit lower); mainly who carries it changes. Below 0° the lower back arches (overextends), as when people lift past straight at the top: the hips bend more for the same trunk position, and the back muscles work short, where they are weaker.

trunk3d.note: 3D view: the trunk muscles of the OpenSim lumbar spine model (Christophy et al. 2012, MIT licence) bent to the lower back's angle and set on the pelvis, shaded by this exercise's muscle effort. Groups the exercise doesn't load stay grey.
